title: Error Detection
body:
The MC68000 implements error detection in the following ways: 

1. Parity Checking: The MC68000 supports parity checking for data and address buses. Parity bits are generated and checked to detect single-bit errors during data transfers.

2. Bus Error Detection: The MC68000 has built-in bus error detection circuitry that monitors the integrity of the bus signals during data transfers. Any discrepancy in the bus signals can trigger a bus error interrupt, allowing the system to handle the error condition.

3. Stack Overflow/Underflow Detection: The MC68000 provides stack overflow and underflow detection mechanisms. These mechanisms monitor the stack pointer to ensure that it stays within the defined stack boundaries. If a stack overflow or underflow is detected, an exception is generated to handle the error condition.

4. Illegal Instruction Detection: The MC68000 includes logic to detect illegal instructions during program execution. If an illegal instruction is encountered, an exception is generated, allowing the system to handle the error condition appropriately.

5. Unimplemented Address Space Detection: The MC68000 has mechanisms to detect accesses to unimplemented memory or I/O locations in its address space. When such accesses occur, an exception is generated, indicating an error condition.

Overall, these error detection mechanisms help ensure reliable and correct operation of the MC68000 processor by detecting and notifying any errors that may occur during data transfers or program execution.


The taxonomy of what these faults look like from the programmer's side, including the bomb
counts, is in [[Assembly Errors]]. A stack overflow usually means runaway [[Recursion]];
see [[Subroutines]].

**Detection is the first rung of three.** Parity notices a single-bit error and cannot repair it.
Repairing it is [[Error Correcting Code]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]], and the algebra both rest
on is [[Finite Field]] in [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101): a parity bit is a linear equation over
$GF(2)$, where addition is XOR, and Reed-Solomon does the same trick over $GF(2^8)$ with a whole
[[Byte]] as the symbol.
